notes.meaning: God raised up Rezon from Zobah as another enemy against Solomon. Rezon had fled from his master King Hadadezer when David defeated the Syrian army. Even though Rezon acted out of personal ambition or revenge, God used him as an instrument to discipline Solomon for his sins.

After David defeated Zobah, Rezon gathered fugitives and became the captain of a raiding band. Eventually, he and his men marched into Damascus, settled there, and took control of the city. This gave Rezon a strong base near Israel's northern border from which to cause trouble.

Rezon remained an enemy of Israel throughout Solomon's reign, adding to the troubles caused by Hadad in the south. While Solomon was faithful, God gave him peace on all sides, but his drift into idolatry left the nation vulnerable to hostile neighbours. Rezon despised Israel and used his power in Damascus to harass Solomon's borders and trade routes.

Jeroboam was an Ephraimite whose widowed mother was named Zeruah. He was one of Solomon's own trusted officials, yet he eventually rebelled against the king. God had previously warned that He would give most of the kingdom to a servant, and Jeroboam was the man chosen for that role.

The background to Jeroboam's rebellion began during Solomon's major building projects in Jerusalem. The king was constructing the supporting terraces called the Millo and closing the gap in the wall around the city of David. These heavy construction projects placed heavy burdens on the people and stirred up deep discontent.

Jeroboam was a capable and energetic young man who stood out as a hard worker. When Solomon saw his skill and diligence, he promoted him to supervise the entire forced labour crew from Ephraim and Manasseh, known as the house of Joseph. This position gave Jeroboam great authority and influence among the northern tribes.

One day, as Jeroboam was walking outside Jerusalem, the prophet Ahijah from Shiloh met him on the road. Ahijah was wearing a brand-new cloak, and the two men were alone in the open field. This private meeting allowed the prophet to deliver God's secret message without interference.

Ahijah grabbed the new cloak he was wearing and tore it into twelve separate pieces. Prophets often acted out their messages with visual signs so people would clearly understand what God was about to do. The tearing of a fresh, strong garment showed that the young and united kingdom of Israel was about to be torn apart.

Ahijah told Jeroboam to take ten of the torn pieces for himself. This meant the Lord was going to tear ten tribes away from Solomon's royal line and hand them to Jeroboam. God gave him this kingdom not because Jeroboam was righteous, but as a judgment on Solomon's idolatry.

God explained that one tribe would stay with David's royal family for the sake of David and Jerusalem. Even though the nation deserved to lose everything, God remained loyal to His covenant promise to David and kept Jerusalem as His chosen place of worship. This showed that God tempers His judgment with mercy.

God stated the reason for this severe judgment: Solomon and many of the people had abandoned the Lord to worship foreign idols like Ashtoreth, Chemosh, and Milcom. They failed to walk in God's ways or keep His laws as David had done. Although David sinned, he never gave his heart away to false gods.

The Lord made it clear that He would not strip the kingdom from Solomon during his lifetime. For the sake of David, who had faithfully kept God's commands, Solomon was permitted to remain ruler until his death. Children often receive earthly blessings and patience from God because of a parent's faithful walk.

The loss of the ten tribes would take place under Solomon's son, and those tribes would be handed over to Jeroboam. The judgment was certain, but God delayed its full execution to the next generation. This also taught Jeroboam that he had to wait for God's timing instead of seizing power immediately.

Solomon's son was to keep one tribe so that David would always have a burning lamp before the Lord in Jerusalem. The lamp represents a continuing line of royal descendants on the throne. This unbroken line ultimately looked forward to the Messiah, who would come from David's family to rule forever.

God promised Jeroboam that he would become king over Israel and receive all the authority his heart desired. The Lord saw Jeroboam's secret ambition and offered to fulfill it in His own way. At the same time, God set boundaries so Jeroboam would know that kingship is a gift from God, not something to grab by force.

The Lord offered Jeroboam an extraordinary conditional promise: if he obeyed God's commands and lived faithfully like David, God would build him a lasting dynasty. Jeroboam had the chance to establish his family permanently over the northern tribes. Sadly, Jeroboam later abandoned God's laws, which led to the ruin of his entire family.

God stated that He would humble David’s descendants because of this sin, but the humiliation would not last forever. The division of the kingdom was a severe chastisement, but God's special promise to David's line remained secure. In time, God's kingdom would find its perfect and eternal restoration in the Messiah.

When Solomon learned of the prophecy and the unrest, he tried to put Jeroboam to death, foolishly thinking he could defeat God's plan. Jeroboam escaped to Egypt and found protection under King Shishak until Solomon died. Unlike David, who refused to lift a hand against King Saul, Jeroboam rushed ahead into rebellion before God's time had arrived.

The writer mentions that the rest of Solomon’s deeds, achievements, and wisdom were recorded in the Book of the Acts of Solomon. This was an official court history kept by royal scribes during his reign. The author of Kings used these reliable historical records under the guidance of the Holy Spirit to write Scripture.

Solomon reigned over all Israel in Jerusalem for forty years, the same length of time as his father David. However, Solomon died at a relatively young age, around sixty, compared to his father. His pursuit of luxury and foreign gods likely cost him the long life that God had originally promised to obedience.

Solomon died and was buried with honor in the city of David, and his son Rehoboam took the throne in his place. The biblical account ends his life without mentioning any clear repentance, leaving behind a solemn reminder of how far a wise person can fall. His divided heart left behind a fractured kingdom that was soon torn in two.

differ.view: Some hold that Solomon definitely repented and was saved, pointing to the book of Ecclesiastes as proof of his late-life repentance and noting God's covenant promise to David that mercy would not depart from his son.
Many teach that Scripture deliberately leaves Solomon's repentance unrecorded so his eternal state remains uncertain to us, serving as a solemn warning against backsliding.
Some teach that because the Bible gives no record of repentance and shows Solomon dying in his apostasy, we cannot assume he was saved.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars observe that the author simply uses the standard royal burial formula and focuses on the covenant consequences for the nation rather than the personal eternal destiny of the king.
